n: A crafty serpent questions God’s command, twisting it to sound harsher than it was. The book of Moses reveals that Satan was speaking through the serpent, seeking to destroy God’s plan.
Eve corrects the serpent: they may eat from the garden’s trees. She knows God has been generous.

f.g: Eve’s reply shows she understood God’s command well.

n: Eve names the one forbidden tree and adds “neither shall ye touch it,” which God did not say in chapter 2. Some readers see a protective fence around the command; others see the rule growing stricter in her mind.
The serpent flatly contradicts God. This is the first lie in scripture, and Jesus later called the devil “a liar, and the father of it.”

Satan mixes truth with deception. Eating would open their eyes and bring knowledge of good and evil—God later confirms this in verse 22—but Satan hides the cost and paints God as withholding good things.

f.w: ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil

n: Eve sees that the fruit is good, beautiful, and promises wisdom, and she eats; Adam eats too. Latter-day Saints view this as a choice that opened mortality and the way to eternal progress, though it brought real consequences.

f.g: Eve was drawn by a desire for wisdom, not mere appetite.

f.w: she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat

n: Their eyes are opened, and they suddenly feel exposed. They try to cover themselves with fig leaves—a human attempt to hide shame that God will soon replace with His own covering.

f.g: Fig leaves are large but brittle—a poor, temporary covering.
Loincloths or coverings for the waist.

n: God comes walking in the garden in the evening breeze, but Adam and Eve hide among the trees. The garden that was a place of fellowship becomes a place of hiding.

f.w: in the cool of the day
f.g: Literally “in the wind (or spirit) of the day”—the breezy evening hours.

n: God calls, “Where art thou?” He knows where Adam is; the question invites Adam to come out and own what he has done. God seeks His children even after they fall.
Adam admits fear and shame. Before, God’s voice brought joy; now it brings fear. Sin changes how we feel in God’s presence.
God asks two pointed questions, giving Adam the chance to confess honestly.

f.g: God’s questions are a gentle form of judgment that invites honesty.

n: Adam blames Eve—and indirectly God, who “gave” her. The blame game begins.

f.w: The woman whom thou gavest to be with me
f.g: Adam shifts responsibility to both Eve and God.

n: Eve says the serpent deceived her. Her answer is more honest about deception, but she too points elsewhere.
God curses the serpent first. Crawling and “eating dust” picture deep humiliation and defeat.

This is often called the first gospel promise. There will be ongoing conflict between Satan and humanity, but a descendant of the woman will crush the serpent’s head while suffering a wound to the heel—a prophecy of Jesus Christ’s victory.

f.g: A fatal, crushing blow, compared to the serpent’s lesser strike at the heel.

n: Eve’s life will now include pain in bearing children, yet also the privilege of motherhood. Her relationship with her husband will also face new strains in a fallen world.

f.g: Hebrew ʿitsavon — pain, toil, hard labor; the same word is used of Adam’s toil in verse 17.
Latter-day Saint leaders have taught that the sense is to preside in love and righteousness, as equal partners, not to dominate.

n: The ground is cursed “for thy sake”—for Adam’s benefit. Hard work in a resistant world will help him grow. Mortal life will be a place of effort and learning.

f.g: Can mean both “because of you” and “for your benefit.”

n: Weeds and thorns will make farming difficult. Thorns later become a symbol of the curse that Christ bore when He wore a crown of thorns.
Life will now require sweaty labor, and death will come: the body returns to the earth it came from. Physical death enters the world through the Fall.

f.w: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return

n: Right after hearing about death, Adam names his wife Eve, “living.” It is an act of hope: through her, life will continue and the promised Seed will come.
God Himself makes garments of skins to clothe them, replacing their fig leaves. An animal’s life was apparently given, and many see here a foreshadowing of Christ’s atoning sacrifice that covers sin.

f.g: The Hebrew word for “atonement” (kippur) has a root linked to covering.

n: Having gained knowledge of good and evil, Adam and Eve must not eat of the tree of life and live forever in their fallen state. Alma explains they needed a probationary time to repent.

f.g: God speaks again in the plural, as in Genesis 1:26.

n: God sends Adam out of Eden to work the ground. Mortal life on the earth now begins.
Cherubim—heavenly guardians—and a flaming sword block the way back to the tree of life. Yet the way is guarded, not destroyed; through Christ, the path back to God’s presence is opened again.

f.g: “Cherubim” is already plural in Hebrew. Images of cherubim later guard the ark of the covenant in the temple.

f.w: the way of the tree of life
